name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare is a structured review of whether a care organization can adopt, deploy, and operate AI tools without breaking its clinical, regulatory, or security obligations. It covers the full lifecycle from intake and vendor review to clinical validation, monitoring, and retirement. It also maps each model or tool to the workflows it touches, the data it consumes, and the decisions it informs. Because the site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 800 scientific models, the audit treats model inventory as a living register rather than a one-time list. It sits inside governance, compliance, and medical device security, so it asks both can this run here and can we prove it remains safe.

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare is a structured review of whether a care organization can adopt, deploy, and operate AI tools without breaking its clinical, regulatory, or security obligations. It covers the full lifecycle from intake and vendor review to clinical validation, monitoring, and retirement. It also maps each model or tool to the workflows it touches, the data it consumes, and the decisions it informs. Because the site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 800 scientific models, the audit treats model inventory as a living register rather than a one-time list. It sits inside governance, compliance, and medical device security, so it asks both can this run here and can we prove it remains safe.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same systems that support clinical operations and AI deployment: electronic health records, data warehouses, cloud or on-premise compute, model registries, and monitoring pipelines. It needs identity and access management, audit logging, version control, and secure data handling for protected health information. For regulated software, it also touches quality management systems, risk files, and post-market surveillance records. The infrastructure must produce evidence that can be reviewed by compliance, security, and clinical teams, not just dashboards for data scientists. Where tools are embedded in devices or third-party platforms, the audit follows the data and control boundaries into those environments.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams start with an inventory and a use-case classification, then run a risk assessment that considers patient impact, autonomy, data sensitivity, and regulatory status. They gather documentation such as intended use, training data provenance, validation results, human oversight plans, and failure modes. They test the tool against local data and workflows, review alerts and overrides, and set thresholds for performance drift. Findings are recorded in a traceable register with owners, deadlines, and evidence links. The method is repeatable, so an audit can be rerun when a model changes, a vendor updates, or a new clinical pathway is added.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The audit examines who is accountable when an AI tool contributes to harm, how consent and data rights are handled, and whether the provenance of training and input data can be demonstrated. It checks contracts, liability terms, indemnities, and incident reporting routes, because the site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies. It also reviews whether the tool is a medical device, a clinical decision support function, or an administrative aid, since that changes the applicable rules. Provenance records in a mature audit cover data sources, labeling, transformations, model versions, and the human review that approved each release. The audit does not resolve legal questions, but it creates the evidence trail that legal, compliance, and clinical leaders need.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The audit is moving from periodic, document-heavy reviews toward continuous assurance, with automated monitoring, model cards, and real-time drift alerts. Regulators and accreditors are asking for stronger post-market surveillance and clearer human oversight, so audit trails will need to be machine-readable and tied to clinical outcomes. As the site's 215 compliance and regulation pages suggest, the rule set is broad and still expanding, which pushes organizations toward shared control libraries and common evidence formats. Expect more attention to generative and agentic tools, where the boundary between a documented model and an emergent workflow is harder to draw. The practical direction is an audit that runs alongside care, not one that arrives months after deployment.
